title: The Intel 4004 and the Birth of the Microprocessor (1971)
explainer: In 1971, Intel engineers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stan Mazor, working with Masatoshi Shima of the Japanese calculator maker Busicom, finished the Intel 4004 — originally meant as one chip in a custom calculator chipset, it instead became the first commercially sold microprocessor: a complete CPU, with roughly 2,300 transistors, on a single piece of silicon. Before the 4004, 'a CPU' meant wiring together many separate chips and discrete components across a board; the 4004 proved that the whole 'calculator' piece of a computer described above could be shrunk onto one chip, which is the actual reason a modern CPU is a single component you can hold between two fingers rather than a cabinet full of boards.

title: Jack Kilby, Robert Noyce, and the Invention of the Integrated Circuit (1958-1959)
explainer: In 1958, Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built the first working integrated circuit — multiple electronic components fabricated together on one piece of semiconductor material instead of wired together as separate parts — and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor independently developed a more manufacturable version in early 1959 using the planar process that became the industry standard. The two companies disputed the patent rights for years before cross-licensing their designs, and both men are now credited as co-inventors (Kilby received the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work). This invention is the reason the motherboard described above is 'wiring' connecting a handful of dense chips, rather than a board covered in thousands of individually wired, loose transistors and resistors.
